p.x:
I live in a house in Ayutthaya with my family. It's not very tall: it has only two floors. The walls are made of brick, and the roof is red. In front of the house there is a small garden and a metal gate.
Inside, there are stairs to the second floor, where the bedrooms are. My bedroom has a balcony, and I can see an old temple from it. The temple is made of stone and has a tall tower.
My grandfather's house is very different. It's a traditional Thai house made of wood, and it stands on high posts. He built it himself fifty years ago! I love visiting him, because the house is cool even on hot days.

Some buildings are so famous that everyone knows them. The Eiffel Tower in Paris was constructed in 1889 for a world fair. Many people thought its steel structure was ugly, and it was supposed to be demolished after twenty years. Today, it is one of the most visited places in the world.
The Colosseum in Rome is almost 2,000 years old. It was built with stone and concrete, and it has many arches. Although parts of it have fallen down, experts have worked hard to restore and preserve it.
In Bangkok, the Grand Palace is famous for its golden roofs and beautiful details, while the Mahanakhon tower, with its unusual shape, is one of the tallest buildings in Thailand. It has 77 storeys, and a fast elevator takes visitors to the top in less than a minute.
Modern architects are also designing eco-friendly buildings. Some have gardens on the roof, and others are made of timber instead of concrete. Strong foundations, wide courtyards and tall columns are old ideas that architects still use today, and many new buildings in hot countries use domes and shady courtyards to stay cool.

Architecture has been called 'the art we live in'. Unlike a painting, a building must do more than look beautiful: it must stand up, keep out the weather and serve the people who use it. The Roman architect Vitruvius summarised these demands as strength, usefulness and beauty.
For centuries, beauty was associated with ornate decoration and classical principles of symmetry and proportion. Grand facades covered in carvings and columns were designed to impress. In the early twentieth century, however, modernist architects rejected this tradition. Famously declaring that 'form follows function', they favoured clean lines, open spaces and new materials such as reinforced concrete and glass. Their influence can still be seen in today's minimalist homes and office towers.
Today, the debate has shifted again. In a warming world, architects are judged not only on appearance but on environmental performance. Traditional buildings in tropical countries, with their high roofs, raised floors and natural ventilation, are being studied for lessons that can reduce the need for air conditioning. Meanwhile, cities compete to build iconic skyscrapers that will define their skyline and attract tourists.
Critics argue that this focus on spectacular individual buildings can distract from urban planning. A beautiful tower may look impressive in photographs, but if it is surrounded by traffic and lacks parks or public spaces, it does little for the people who live nearby. Great architecture, they suggest, begins not with a blueprint for a single building, but with a vision for the whole city.
